title: Soft threshold surge chronicle
content:
(personal scratchpad) — motivation and running notes

Why I ran this: we see frequent short (~10s–30s) ingress spikes that clip p95/p99 even when steady qps is fine. Hard preemption/clamp policies help avoid overload but cause large tail spikes and retries. Idea: implement a soft-threshold window (per-tenant rolling leaky bucket) that probabilistically shapes or delays a small fraction of requests instead of wholesale reject or preempt. Want to characterize effect on latency vs. throughput vs. error rate under synthetic surge arrivals.

Setup summary (quick):
- Cluster: dedicated test pool, 4x A10G (driver: nvidia-520), 64GB RAM per node
- Model: redwood-micro-13b-quant (FP16-ish sim), seq_len=512 typical, KVcache present
- Serving runtime build: local branch soft-threshold-probe (PR 789) with a configurable window size and shaping probability curve
- Client driver: modified wrk-like harness that can emit Poisson arrivals and manual spikes; records p50/p90/p95/p99 and error counts per-second
- Cache state: warm (100 recent keys primed) or cold (cold start from disk) toggles used per run

Parameters varied:
- baseline: no shaping, hard-threshold=concurrency=64
- soft-threshold window sizes: 10s, 30s, 60s (rolling)
- shaping policy: linear-prob (prob of delay grows linearly from 0 -> 0.5 across window), sigmoid-prob (gentler), and aggressive (0->0.9)
- spike profile: microburst (500 qps for 12s), sawtooth (ramp 0->400 qps over 20s then drop), sustained bump (200 qps for 120s)
- client concurrency: 64 clients, request payloads randomized to simulate 75–125 token outputs

Primary metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), tail-latency tail area (integral above p95 during spike), error rate (5xx + throttles), throughput (requests/s), retry amplification (retries triggered by client).

Representative run table (condensed) — all runs warm cache unless noted:

Config | Spike | p50 | p95 | p99 | err% | rps
-------|-------|-----|-----|-----|------|-----
baseline (no shaping) | microburst 500qps x12s | 38ms | 420ms | 1230ms | 1.6% | 480
soft-10s linear-0.5 | same | 45ms | 220ms | 430ms | 0.9% | 460
soft-30s sigmoid-0.5 | same | 52ms | 190ms | 360ms | 0.6% | 455
soft-60s aggressive-0.9 | same | 68ms | 160ms | 280ms | 1.1% | 430
baseline | sawtooth ramp | 36ms | 310ms | 980ms | 1.2% | 420
soft-30s sigmoid | sawtooth | 48ms | 210ms | 410ms | 0.7% | 400
soft-30s sigmoid cold-cache | microburst | 120ms | 620ms | 1800ms | 4.6% | 300

Notes on table (hand-summary):
- Soft shaping consistently reduces p95/p99 substantially compared to baseline for the same peak injection (roughly 2–4x improvement at p99 under microbursts), at a modest cost to p50 and sustained throughput.
- Aggressive shaping pushes more load into delays (higher p50) but can reduce spikes at p99 more. However aggressive shows slightly higher error% (likely client timeouts/retries).
- Cold cache magnifies everything — shaping helps but cannot fully mask backend cold penalties (see cold-cache run).

Per-second time-resolved observation (microburst, soft-30s sigmoid):
- t=0–2s: ingress ramping, no shaping triggered yet (below window baseline)
- t=3–8s: shaping probability rises to ~0.35, observed steady de-prioritization for ~30% of requests -> visible smoothing in qps at server side
- t=9–12s: peak arrival; server-side concurrent inflight stays near configured concurrency cap; p99 plateau ~350–420ms (vs 1.2s baseline)
- t>12s: shaping throttles fall; backlog drains in ~4s due to short delays. No retry storms observed because client retry window set to 2s.

Raw traces (snippets):
- baseline p99 spikes correlated with enqueue depth hitting 150–200 (kernel accept queue + internal work queue).
- with soft shaping, queue never exceeds ~80 items; more consistent dispatching to GPUs.

Unresolved/interesting behaviours:
- Retry amplification: when shaping probability is high, some clients (older SDK) immediately retry on perceived timeouts causing bursty reentry. We need a client-side backoff recommendation.
- Multi-tenant fairness: tenant with high-weight requests gets preferential serving even under shaping because of priority lanes — need to test tenant-aware soft thresholds.
- Warmup interaction: the shape window interacts badly with warmup heuristics that pre-warm KVcache; in some runs shaping prevented timely warm-cache priming, making first 30s after a spike worse.

Quick conclusions / takeaways (draft):
- Soft-threshold shaping is promising: tradeoff is small increase in median latency and small throughput hit for large improvements to tail latency and error rates during short surges.
- Sigmoid-style probability curve with moderate max (~0.5) and 20–40s window seems to give best p99/p95 wins without explosive retry amplification.
- Must pair shaping with: (a) client-side gentle backoff guidance, (b) tenant-aware shaping knobs, (c) a warm-cache exemption window for priming traffic.

Action items / TODOs (self):
- [ ] Run tenant-weighted experiments: ensure low-volume customers aren't starved; create synthetic 2-tenant test. (assign to Luca)
- [ ] Prototype client SDK change to add jittered exponential backoff for 500/429 responses (Samira to help)
- [ ] Add instrumentation: per-tenant shaping hit-rate, delayed-request queue length, and correlation with KVcache misses
- [ ] Smoke test soft-threshold in Dedicated staging 8x H100 pool (lower-level hardware effect)

Notes to self:
- Keep PR 789 small; feature flag default OFF. We want to get ops buy-in before turning on in any prod pool.
- Add a short explainer in runtime README: what shaping means for developers — include recommended retry interval (>= 2.5s)

Slack snippets to paste later: "soft-threshold prototype cut p99 by ~3x for short bursts in warm-cache tests; trade is ~10–40ms p50 increase depending on config. Need client backoff to avoid retry storms."

References / links:
- INF-3142 (experiment tracking)
- runtime PR #789 (soft-threshold branch)
- spreadsheet: surge-tests-2024-Q4 (internal drive sheet id: sheet:AB12)

Endnotes: this is rough; save as draft and link to the more formal experiment writeup later. Felt useful to capture the incremental behaviours (queue shapes, interaction with warm-cache, client retries) — these were not obvious until I looked at per-second traces.

-- Kaiya
